_comment: Trigstation directory service — protocol v1 API conformance vectors for DIRECTORY-SPEC.md §5. Generated by cmd/gen-api-vectors; regenerating must reproduce this file byte for byte.
_warning: TEST ONLY. Every key here is derived from a counting sequence hashed with a published domain string. They are reproducible by anyone and secret to nobody.

Every expectation is evaluated against the fixed clock in `now`, never against wall time. A harness that uses its own clock will see records expire and fixtures fail for reasons that have nothing to do with conformance.

Each fixture is driven against a freshly built instance holding the declared initial state. Fixtures whose `mutates_state` is true change what the instance holds, so a harness that cannot reset between fixtures must run those last and cannot claim order independence.

pow_bits is 8 here, not the default 20. §6.1 makes it an instance parameter, and verification costs one SHA-256 at any difficulty — only solving is exponential. The shipped default is exercised by testdata/vectors.json.

encoding._note: How a value in this file becomes bytes on the wire. Nothing here assumes a language, a routing library or a JSON implementation.
encoding.binary_values: Binary values outside request and response bodies — channel identifiers, lookup identifiers — are unpadded base64url, RFC 4648 §5, canonically encoded per §4.4. No '=' is ever emitted.
encoding.bodies: Every request and response body is an object carrying its own encoding, so that a binary body and a JSON body are read the same way. A body that is meant to be absent says so explicitly rather than being omitted.

body_encodings.name: empty
body_encodings.note: No body at all. Send nothing; expect zero bytes.

body_encodings.name: utf8
body_encodings.note: `value` is the body, character for character, encoded as UTF-8. Used for JSON bodies so that whitespace and member order are visible to a reader.

body_encodings.name: base64url
body_encodings.note: `value` decodes as unpadded base64url to the body bytes. Used where the body is binary or contains bytes no text encoding should be trusted with.

body_encodings.name: repeated_byte
body_encodings.note: The single byte `byte` (0–255, absent means 0) repeated `length` times. Used for the payload-limit fixtures, where writing 64 KiB of literal data into this file would obscure everything around it.

comparisons.name: empty
comparisons.note: The response must carry no body bytes.

comparisons.name: exact_bytes
comparisons.note: The response body must equal the expected bytes exactly.

comparisons.name: json_object
comparisons.note: The response must be a JSON object equal to the expected one. Member order is not significant in JSON and is not compared.

comparisons.name: records_array
comparisons.note: The response must be a JSON object whose only member is `records`, an array whose elements are the expected elements as a multiset — each compared as **bytes**, not as parsed values. §5.2 requires the bytes returned to be the bytes received, and a comparison of parsed values is exactly the comparison that passes with a re-serialising directory. The order of `records` is not significant (§5.3); the expected body is written in the RECOMMENDED order, ascending lookup_id.

encoding.headers: Request headers are sent as given. Header names are case-insensitive per RFC 9110. `expect.headers` must match exactly, `expect.header_tokens` names headers whose comma-separated value must contain every token listed — order, spacing and additional tokens are not significant — and `expect.headers_absent` must not appear at all.
encoding.query: `query` is the raw query string without a leading '?', to be appended to `path` unmodified. It is raw rather than a map because §5.3 requires a repeated parameter to be rejected rather than resolved, and a map cannot express one.

conditions.name: accepted
conditions.note: §5.2 — the publish was accepted and stored.

conditions.name: rate_limited
conditions.note: §5.2 and §5.4 — the source's allowance for this class is spent.

conditions.name: too_large
conditions.note: §5.2 — the received body exceeds max_record_bytes, measured as transmitted.

conditions.name: malformed
conditions.note: §5.2 — not well-formed JSON, a required member absent or null, a duplicate member, a value that is not valid unpadded canonical base64url, or a fixed-width field of the wrong decoded length.

conditions.name: ttl_too_long
conditions.note: §5.2 — expires_at exceeds now + max_ttl, after the skew grace.

conditions.name: sig_invalid
conditions.note: §5.2 — sig does not verify under wk_pub.

conditions.name: expired
conditions.note: §5.2 — expires_at is not strictly greater than the directory's current time.

conditions.name: not_newer
conditions.note: §5.2 — expires_at is not strictly greater than that of an unexpired stored record under the same lookup_id.

conditions.name: empty
conditions.note: §5.4 — the long-poll window elapsed with no blob.

conditions.name: bad_channel
conditions.note: §5.4 — channel_id is not exactly 32 bytes of unpadded base64url.

conditions.name: conflict
conditions.note: §5.4 — the channel already holds an unexpired blob.

conditions.name: signal_too_large
conditions.note: §5.4 — the body exceeds the §4.3 signal channel payload limit.

evaluation_order.note: The conditions MUST be evaluated in this order and the directory MUST return the code of the first that fails. Without a fixed order a request violating two conditions receives a different code from different directories, and a publisher's retry logic — driven entirely by the code — diverges accordingly. The order is also cheapest-first: the two SHA-256 checks precede the Ed25519 verification, which costs roughly two orders of magnitude more.
§5.3 binds every rejection to 400 and gives no evaluation order, so the choice between two reasons can never be observed on the wire.

The conditions of the §5.4 table are disjoint, so their order carries no meaning. The one exception is not an ordering: an instance that is disabled answers 404 without regard to anything else about the request.

_note: Build an instance from the named entry in `instances`, load `initial_state` into it, run any `prior_requests`, then issue `request` and compare the response against `expect`.

Load the records by issuing the PUT given in each initial_state.records[] entry, with the instance's clock reading `loaded_at`; each returns 204. A directory that loads its state some other way MUST store the envelope bytes verbatim.

Load the signal channels by issuing a POST of each blob to its channel_id with the instance's clock reading `posted_at`; each returns 204. One channel is loaded in the past so that its blob has expired by `now`.
Reset the instance between fixtures. Every fixture is then order-independent: none depends on a state another leaves behind.

instances.name: default
note: A conforming instance holding the declared initial state, with allowances high enough that no fixture reaches them.

signal_poll_window_maximum is the §5.4 ceiling, not a setting: a directory MUST NOT hold a long-poll open for longer, and SHOULD hold it for the full 30 seconds for real clients. A conformance harness MAY shorten it, because the GET-with-no-blob fixture asserts the status and not the duration.

instances.name: signal-disabled
note: The same instance with signal channels off, which is the only configuration in which §5.4 answers 404. It holds the same records, so its GET /v1/meta reports the same record_count.

instances.name: draining
note: The same instance after it has begun a graceful shutdown: still listening, no longer able to broker a rendezvous. §5.4 binds this to 429 for either method — the same code as at capacity, because the client's correct response is the same.
Draining releases every in-flight long-poll and drops every stored blob, so the pre-loaded channels are gone by the time a fixture runs against this instance.

instances.name: limits-of-one
note: An instance whose per-class allowance is one request per window, and which holds no initial state — loading it would spend the allowance the fixtures exist to spend deliberately.
The rate-limit rows of §5.2 and §5.4 cannot be expressed by a single request, so they are expressed as this instance plus a prior request that spends the class's allowance.
§6.4 counts the three classes independently, and the fixtures rely on it: a prior GET spends nothing a POST needs.

_note: 40 records and 2 signal channels. The record count is exactly 2 × k_min, which is the smallest instance on which §5.3's cap — max(0, floor(log2(record_count / k_min))) — is greater than zero, and therefore the smallest on which a masked prefix query can be shown to work at all.

Every identifier here begins with a 1 bit. That is deliberate: at a cap of 1 bit the only queries available are bits = 0 and bits = 1, and a table whose identifiers all share their first bit answers the two halves of that query with the whole table and with nothing — which is what makes both the matching case and §5.3's empty-result shape observable on an instance small enough to ship as a fixture.
One record is stored with formatting a re-serialising directory would destroy. Every response that contains it is byte-exact only if the directory reproduced the bytes it received.
Records are given as the exact bytes a publisher sent, and §5.2 requires those bytes to be what §5.3 returns.

signal_channels.note: Holds an unexpired blob at now. This is the channel §5.4's first-write-wins rule applies to, and the one a GET delivers.

Loaded far enough in the past that its blob has expired at now. §5.4 rejects a second write only where the channel holds an *unexpired* blob, so a POST here is stored. Load it with the instance's clock reading posted_at, then return the clock to now.

blob.value: a blob that has outlived its TTL

_note: §5.5 requires Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every /v1/ response — including the ones no handler produces, such as a 404 for an unregistered path under /v1/ and a 405 for a method that is not one of the four. A browser cannot read an error it is not allowed to see.

A wildcard origin is safe here in a way it is not for most services, because the API carries no ambient authority: no cookies, no credentials, no session, and every write is authorised by a signature in the body.
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials MUST NOT be sent, from anywhere, on any response.
These are asserted on every fixture in this file rather than restated on each.
response_invariants.applies_to: every response to a request whose path begins with /v1/

fixtures.row: All seven members are REQUIRED
note: record_count is the true count of unexpired records here because §5.1's RECOMMENDED reduction — round down to two significant figures — leaves a count below 100 unchanged.
§5.1 permits record_count to be understated and forbids it from ever exceeding the true count, so a harness whose instance rounds differently should assert record_count <= 40 rather than equality.
source_url MUST point at the source of the running instance. Configure the instance with the value declared under instances[] to compare exactly; only its non-emptiness is normative.

fixtures.row: An instance that does not broker signal channels advertises "signal": false
note: The member is emitted, not omitted. An instance with signal channels off is exactly the instance a client most needs to be told about, and a client that saw no member would discover the answer as a 404 it is entitled to read as "try another directory".

fixtures.row: Accepted and stored
note: Every condition passes: the body is inside max_record_bytes, v is 1, expires_at is in the future and inside max_ttl, lookup_id is SHA-256(wk_pub), the proof of work meets pow_bits, the signature verifies under wk_pub, and no record is stored under this lookup_id.
There is no response body for any §5.2 outcome. The code is the whole answer.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST NOT reject a request on the basis of its Content-Type
note: The RECOMMENDED type. A browser publishing with it is forced into a CORS preflight, which is why §5.5 requires one.
Rejecting on the header gains nothing, because the body is validated in full regardless, and costs interoperability with constrained clients.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST NOT reject a request on the basis of its Content-Type
note: application/json is acceptable.
Rejecting on the header gains nothing, because the body is validated in full regardless, and costs interoperability with constrained clients.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST NOT reject a request on the basis of its Content-Type
note: An unrecognised type is acceptable.
Rejecting on the header gains nothing, because the body is validated in full regardless, and costs interoperability with constrained clients.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST NOT reject a request on the basis of its Content-Type
note: An absent header is acceptable. The body is validated in full either way.
Rejecting on the header gains nothing, because the body is validated in full regardless, and costs interoperability with constrained clients.

fixtures.row: Rate limited
note: Rate limiting is the first row of the §5.2 order, and it is first so that a flood costs the directory as little as possible: the limit is applied before the body is read, let alone parsed or measured.

A fixture cannot express "already rate limited" in one request. It is expressed here as an instance whose per-class allowance is 1 and a prior request of the same class that spends it. The prior request is deliberately one that changes no state.
§6.4 counts PUT /v1/record, GET /v1/record and signal channel access independently, so spending this allowance must not affect the other two.

prior_requests.note: Spends this source's single PUT allowance. Its own outcome is 400 and it stores nothing.

fixtures.row: Accepted and stored
note: The body is exactly max_record_bytes (4096) as transmitted. The limit is a maximum, not a bound to stay under.
The padding is an unknown member, which §10 requires a directory to ignore rather than reject.

fixtures.row: Received body exceeds max_record_bytes
note: The body is max_record_bytes + 1 (4097) as transmitted. One byte is the whole difference between this fixture and the one before it.
Measured before any parsing, so a directory never has to buffer an oversized body to answer.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: The body is not JSON at all.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: An empty body is not a well-formed envelope. It is worth stating because an empty body is what a client library produces when a serialisation step silently fails.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: Well-formed JSON, but not an object. An envelope is an object (§4.1).

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: pow is absent. Every one of the eight members of §4.1 is needed to evaluate §5.2, so an envelope missing any of them is malformed rather than merely unusual.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: pow is present with the value null. §5.2: an explicit null is not a value — a required member present with the value null MUST be treated exactly as an absent member.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: lookup_id is the padded spelling of the same 32 bytes. §4.4 requires padded input to be rejected as malformed rather than stripped, because a directory stores and returns envelopes verbatim: anything it tolerates it hands unchanged to every client that queries. Tolerance here does not contain a malformed encoding, it distributes one.
Java's Base64.getUrlEncoder and Python's urlsafe_b64encode pad by default, so this is among the first things an implementer on those platforms gets wrong.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: lookup_id decodes to the right 32 bytes but its final character carries non-zero unused bits. A 32-byte value occupies 43 characters carrying 258 bits, so without §4.4's canonical-encoding rule there are four spellings of every such value — all of which verify, and all of which would be served.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: nonce decodes to 11 bytes where §4.1 fixes 12. A fixed-width field that decodes to the wrong length is malformed, not merely unusual: the signing input of §4.1 is a bare concatenation, and its injectivity depends on every field before ct having its declared width.

fixtures.row: Body is not well-formed JSON, a required member is absent, a value is not valid unpadded base64url, or a fixed-width field decodes to the wrong length
note: expires_at appears twice. §5.2 requires this to be rejected rather than resolved: parsers disagree about which occurrence wins — Go takes the last, many others the first — and because a directory verifies a signature over the fields it parsed and then stores the bytes verbatim, a first-wins directory and a last-wins client can end up disagreeing about an expires_at the directory never validated.
That is a signature bypass wearing a parser disagreement as a costume.

fixtures.row: v is not 1
note: v is 2 on a /v1/ path. §4.1 is explicit that this is a rejection rather than an application of the unknown-field rule: v pins the format, so it is not an unknown field.
Every other unrecognised member is ignored (§10), which is what makes an additive change to v1 deployable at all.

fixtures.row: Accepted and stored
note: expires_at is now + max_ttl + 300, exactly the grace §5.2 asks a directory to allow above max_ttl before rejecting.

The grace exists because expires_at is computed from the publisher's clock and evaluated against the directory's, and neither party can observe the other's. Servers SHOULD leave headroom and directories SHOULD allow grace — both, not either: one alone still permits the failure, which presents as a directory rejecting every publish for no visible reason.

fixtures.row: expires_at exceeds now + max_ttl
note: One second beyond the grace. Everything else about this envelope is valid.

An over-long TTL is 400 despite also concerning expires_at, because its remedy differs from the 409 rows: reduce the configured TTL and re-solve the proof of work, rather than republish with a later expiry.

fixtures.row: lookup_id is not SHA-256(wk_pub)
note: lookup_id is a valid 32-byte identifier belonging to a different key. The proof of work is solved over the identifier as stated and the signature verifies under wk_pub, so this fixture violates the binding and nothing else.
One SHA-256 settles it, which is why §5.2 puts it ahead of the Ed25519 verification: a flooding client is rejected on the cheap check.

fixtures.row: pow does not satisfy pow_bits
note: SHA-256("trig-pow-v1" || lookup_id || expires_at || pow) has fewer than 8 leading zero bits, with expires_at and pow each 8 bytes big-endian per §0.1.
pow is not part of the envelope signing input (§4.1), so the signature on this envelope is valid: this fixture violates the proof of work and nothing else.

fixtures.row: sig does not verify under wk_pub
note: A syntactically valid 64-byte Ed25519 signature made with a different key, over the correct canonical bytes. The signature is the authorisation: there is no header to check and no account to consult.
It is the most expensive check in the pipeline by roughly two orders of magnitude, which is why §5.2 puts it last of the cryptographic three.

fixtures.row: expires_at is not strictly greater than the directory's current time
note: expires_at is exactly now. §5.2: a record is live if and only if expires_at is strictly greater than the directory's current time; at equality it is absent.
Equality is not a corner worth leaving open — §5.2's requirement that two conforming directories return identical results is not a guarantee if it has a one-second hole in it.

fixtures.row: expires_at is not strictly greater than the directory's current time
note: One second before now. 409 rather than 400 because the remedy is the publisher's to apply and is the same as the recency rule's: republish with a later expiry, one branch in the publisher rather than two.

fixtures.row: expires_at is not strictly greater than that of an unexpired stored record under the same lookup_id
note: A byte-for-byte replay of the record already stored under this lookup_id. Within an epoch the write key is stable, so a captured earlier envelope still verifies — the recency rule is what stops a replay silently rolling the server's published address back until the next republish, where the rollback would present as a stale address rather than an error.
Strictly greater: equal is rejected.

fixtures.row: expires_at is not strictly greater than that of an unexpired stored record under the same lookup_id
note: An expiry one second below the stored record's, and still comfortably in the future — so this fixture fails the recency rule and not the future-expiry check above it.

fixtures.row: Accepted and stored
note: One second above the stored record's expiry is enough. On success the record replaces the existing one under the same lookup_id — there is one record per lookup_id (§4.3).
This fixture mutates state: after it, the record served under this identifier is this one.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: two conditions violated
note: The body is max_record_bytes + 1 bytes and is not well-formed JSON. Size is row 3 and malformation row 4, so the answer is 413.
An implementation that parses before measuring answers 400 here, and it is right about the body and wrong about the protocol: the size check exists so that an oversized body is never parsed.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: two conditions violated
note: lookup_id is not SHA-256(wk_pub) (row 7) and expires_at equals now (row 10). The answer is 403.

The two codes carry different remedies — 403 means the envelope is wrong, 409 means republish with a later expiry — so a directory that answered 409 would send a conforming publisher into a retry loop it can never escape.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: two conditions violated
note: The signature does not verify (row 9) and the expiry does not exceed the stored record's (row 11). The answer is 403.

The recency rule is last in the order because it is the only condition requiring a storage read. A rejected publish never touches the database, which is also why this fixture leaves the stored record untouched.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: three conditions violated
note: expires_at is beyond max_ttl plus the skew grace (row 6), the proof of work is insufficient (row 8) and the signature does not verify (row 9). The answer is 400.
This is the case where an implementation ordering by cost alone diverges: both 403 conditions are cheaper to reach than they look, and neither may be evaluated first.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: four conditions violated
note: v is 2 (row 5), lookup_id is not SHA-256(wk_pub) (row 7), the proof of work is insufficient (row 8) and the signature does not verify (row 9). The answer is 400.
Three of the four violations draw 403, so an implementation that evaluated the cryptographic conditions first would answer 403 consistently and look entirely reasonable doing it.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: four conditions violated
note: The source's allowance is spent (row 2), the body is over max_record_bytes (row 3), v is 2 (row 5) and expires_at equals now (row 10). The answer is 429.

Rate limiting is first in the order precisely so that none of the work below it is done. An implementation that answered 413 here has read and measured a body it was entitled to drop, which is the cost the ordering exists to avoid.

prior_requests.note: Spends this source's single PUT allowance without storing anything.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: two conditions violated, same code
note: The proof of work is insufficient (row 8) and the signature does not verify (row 9). Both draw 403, so this fixture cannot detect an implementation that evaluates them in the wrong order — and it says so rather than implying a check it does not perform.

It is here because §5.2's ordering argument rests on this pair: the SHA-256 precedes the Ed25519 verification, which costs roughly two orders of magnitude more. The order is unobservable on the wire and load-bearing under flood.

fixtures.row: Evaluation order: two conditions violated, same code
note: expires_at equals now (row 10) and does not exceed the stored record's expiry (row 11). Both draw 409, deliberately: §5.2 groups codes by the publisher's remedy, and the remedy for both is the same — republish with a later expiry, one branch in the publisher rather than two.
So this fixture also cannot discriminate, and is not intended to.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST accept both ?prefix=&bits=0 and ?bits=0 with prefix absent
note: bits = 0 with prefix supplied empty. This is the query every conforming client sends to an instance too small to provide an anonymity set, and it returns the whole table.
The response contains the adversarially formatted record, so it is byte-exact only if the directory reproduced the stored bytes rather than re-serialising them (§5.2).

The order of records is not significant and clients MUST NOT depend on it. The expected body is written in the RECOMMENDED order — ascending lookup_id — because a byte comparison needs one; compare the elements as a multiset if your instance orders differently.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST accept both ?prefix=&bits=0 and ?bits=0 with prefix absent
note: The other spelling. An absent prefix and an empty prefix are the same query at bits = 0, and a directory must accept both — a distinction url.Values-style APIs cannot express in the value alone, which is why it is stated.

fixtures.row: Returns every non-expired envelope whose lookup_id begins with the given bit prefix
note: prefix=8 at bits=1 selects identifiers whose first bit is 1, which is every record in this instance. The padding bits of the character are zero here, so this is the plain case.
This instance holds 40 records, so §5.3's cap is max(0, floor(log2(40 / k_min))) = 1 with the normative k_min of 20. bits = 0 and bits = 1 are accepted and anything wider is 400.
The response contains the adversarially formatted record, so it is byte-exact only if the directory reproduced the stored bytes rather than re-serialising them (§5.2).

fixtures.row: Where bits is not a multiple of four a directory MUST mask and ignore the trailing bits
note: prefix=f at bits=1 carries one significant bit — 1 — and three padding bits that are all set. Masked, it is the same query as prefix=8, and it returns the same records.

A directory that rejected non-zero padding bits answers 400 here, and a directory that compared the character rather than the masked bits answers with an empty array. Both are wrong on the ordinary path rather than on an edge case: at 100,000 records the RECOMMENDED bits is 10, which occupies three hex characters and leaves two bits unused.

fixtures.row: prefix is hex, case-insensitive
note: The same query as the one before it, spelled in upper case. Directories MUST accept both a3f and A3F.

fixtures.row: A directory with no matching records returns 200 with an empty records array, never 404
note: prefix=0 at bits=1 selects identifiers whose first bit is 0, and this instance holds none.
200 with an empty array, never 404. A 404 would tell a client the directory has nothing to say about anything, when what it has is nothing in this bucket.

fixtures.row: Where bits is not a multiple of four a directory MUST mask and ignore the trailing bits
note: prefix=7 at bits=1 masks to the same query as prefix=0: one significant bit of 0, three padding bits that are set. The empty array is the correct answer, and a 400 is not.

fixtures.row: Directories MUST enforce a maximum bits and reject over-precise queries with 400
note: bits = 2 exceeds this instance's cap of 1. This instance holds 40 records, so §5.3's cap is max(0, floor(log2(40 / k_min))) = 1 with the normative k_min of 20. bits = 0 and bits = 1 are accepted and anything wider is 400.
A client asking for a 32-bit prefix has defeated the entire privacy design; the server-side cap is what makes the anonymity set a protocol guarantee rather than a client courtesy.

The cap is computed against the true record count, not the figure §5.1 permits an instance to understate — which is what makes §5.1's promise unconditional that a client following the advertised count can never be rejected here.

fixtures.row: bits is REQUIRED
note: bits is REQUIRED and a directory MUST NOT infer it from the length of prefix. Inference is the tempting shortcut and the one that breaks interoperability silently: it makes a3f mean 12 bits everywhere, so a client that meant 10 gets a narrower bucket and a smaller anonymity set than it asked for, with nothing reporting an error.

fixtures.row: bits is one or more ASCII digits: no sign, no leading zeros
note: A leading zero is two spellings of one value, which is the defect §4.4's canonical-encoding rule closes for base64url. It is rejected here rather than normalised.

fixtures.row: bits is one or more ASCII digits
note: No other notation.

fixtures.row: bits is one or more ASCII digits: no sign
note: No sign. A directory that parsed this as a signed integer and then sized a buffer from it has a worse problem than a 400.

fixtures.row: bits MUST NOT exceed 256, the width of a lookup_id
note: 257 bits with a correctly sized prefix of 65 hex characters, so the only thing wrong with the query is its width.

On this instance the cap of 1 rejects it first, and both bind to 400, so the code cannot say which rule applied. The 256 bound is stated in §5.3 so that an implementation sizing a buffer from the parameter has something to size it against.

fixtures.row: A directory MUST reject any character outside [0-9a-fA-F] with 400
note: 'g' is outside the hex alphabet. Every character is validated, including one whose bits the mask would discard entirely.

fixtures.row: prefix MUST contain exactly ceil(bits / 4) hex characters
note: Two characters where one is required. Too many carries bits the client did not declare.

fixtures.row: prefix MUST contain exactly ceil(bits / 4) hex characters
note: An empty prefix is only meaningful at bits = 0.

fixtures.row: prefix MUST contain exactly ceil(bits / 4) hex characters
note: An absent prefix with bits above zero. The pair of this and the bits = 0 fixtures is what pins the one place absence and emptiness differ.

fixtures.row: A query supplying prefix or bits more than once MUST be rejected rather than resolved
note: Both occurrences agree, and it is still rejected. HTTP stacks disagree about which occurrence wins, so resolving one means two directories reading the same query differently — the failure mode of duplicate JSON members in §5.2. Failing closed on the ambiguity costs nothing, because no honest client emits one.

fixtures.row: A query supplying prefix or bits more than once MUST be rejected rather than resolved
note: Here the two occurrences disagree, which is the case where resolving it silently changes the anonymity set the client asked for.

fixtures.row: Rate limited
note: §6.2 gives GET /v1/record its own allowance, counted independently of publishes and of signal channel access.

§5.3 has no status table of its own and states no code for a rate-limited lookup. 429 is what §5.2 and §5.4 bind rate limiting to, and it is the only code whose remedy — back off or move on — is the right one here.
This instance holds no records, so the prior request returns an empty array; the allowance is spent either way.

prior_requests.note: Spends this source's single GET /v1/record allowance.

fixtures.row: POST — Stored
note: A channel holding nothing accepts the write. The directory treats the body as bytes and MUST NOT attempt to parse, validate or interpret it.

fixtures.row: POST — Stored
note: This channel holds a blob that expired before now. §5.4 rejects a second write only where the channel already holds an *unexpired* blob, so this is a first write.
Expiry is a property of the blob and the clock, not of sweep scheduling — the same rule §5.2 states for records.

fixtures.row: POST — Stored
note: A body of exactly the §4.3 signal channel payload limit, 65536 bytes. The body is the single byte 0x61 repeated; see encoding.body_encodings.

fixtures.row: POST — body exceeds the §4.3 signal channel payload limit
note: One byte over the limit: 65537 bytes.

fixtures.row: POST — channel already holds an unexpired blob
note: The channel holds an unexpired blob, and the stored blob is left untouched.

This is a security property rather than an error case. Under overwrite semantics anyone who guessed or observed a channel identifier could replace a legitimate blob with their own, turning the rendezvous into an injection point; failing closed reduces that to a denial of service the participants detect immediately.

fixtures.row: POST — channel_id is not exactly 32 bytes of unpadded base64url
note: A channel_id is 32 bytes, base64url: exactly 43 unpadded characters.

fixtures.row: POST — channel_id is not exactly 32 bytes of unpadded base64url
note: The padded spelling of the same 32 bytes. §4.4 forbids emitting padding and requires padded input to be rejected rather than stripped.

fixtures.row: POST — channel_id is not exactly 32 bytes of unpadded base64url
note: 43 characters decoding to the right 32 bytes, but with non-zero unused bits in the final character. §5.4 identifies a channel by its decoded bytes, not by the text that spelled them: an implementation keying on the text would treat two spellings as two channels and accept a second write where a conforming directory returns 409. The canonical-encoding rule of §4.4 closes the same gap from the other side, and both apply.

fixtures.row: GET — blob present
note: The blob is returned exactly as posted, including its NUL bytes, its 0xff and the three characters a JSON encoder would rewrite. The directory MUST NOT interpret the body.
Content-Type is application/octet-stream: a directory forbidden to interpret the body must not claim a type for it.
Delivery is destructive — this fixture mutates state, and a second GET on this channel would long-poll.

fixtures.row: GET — long-poll window elapsed with no blob
note: 204, deliberately not 404. A client's correct response to 204 is to poll again; to 404, to try a different directory. Conflating them means a client either hammers an instance that will never answer or abandons one that would have, and PAIRING-SPEC.md §6.3 has both devices polling as its normal path.
The response arrives after the instance's long-poll window elapses, which §5.4 caps at 30 seconds. A conformance harness MAY shorten the window: this fixture asserts the status, not the duration.

fixtures.row: GET — channel_id is not exactly 32 bytes of unpadded base64url
note: 42 characters: one short of the 43 an unpadded 32-byte value occupies. The identifier is checked before the channel is looked up, so no channel is created by a malformed request.

fixtures.row: either — rate limited
note: POST and GET on a signal channel share one allowance (§6.4), so the prior request here is a GET and it is the POST that is refused.
The prior request is a GET with a malformed channel_id, which spends the allowance without long-polling and without creating a channel.

prior_requests.note: Spends this source's single signal allowance.

fixtures.row: either — rate limited
note: The same allowance from the other side: a POST spends it and the GET is refused.

prior_requests.note: Spends this source's single signal allowance.

fixtures.row: either — instance at capacity, or shutting down
note: An instance that is full or draining answers 429, not 204 and not 404. 204 would tell the client to poll again immediately, hot-looping against an instance that has just declined it; 404 would tell the client this directory does not broker signal channels at all — which is wrong, and sticky, because a client that believes it will stop asking.
A harness with no way to drive its instance into this state cannot run this fixture. That is a property of the harness rather than of the directory, and the row is normative either way.

fixtures.row: either — instance at capacity, or shutting down
note: The same on the read side, and it returns promptly rather than holding the poll open: a graceful shutdown must not wait 30 seconds on an idle poller.

fixtures.row: either — instance advertises "signal": false
note: 404 is the one outcome in the §5.4 table that means "this directory does not broker signal channels", and it is reserved for the instance that advertises so in GET /v1/meta.

fixtures.row: either — instance advertises "signal": false
note: The same on the read side. Pairing the advertised capability with the behaviour of the route matters: a client that believes a directory brokers signal channels and finds 404 will stop trying it altogether.

fixtures.row: OPTIONS preflight
note: §5.2 RECOMMENDS publishers send the vendor media type, which is precisely what forces a browser to preflight every publish.
OPTIONS is HTTP transport mechanics for the four operations of §5. It is not a fifth operation and does not bear on the constraint in §10.
Access-Control-Allow-Methods is compared as a token set: the header must list every method given, and order and spacing are not significant.

fixtures.row: OPTIONS preflight
note: The preflight is per route, and §5.5 names this one explicitly.
OPTIONS is HTTP transport mechanics for the four operations of §5. It is not a fifth operation and does not bear on the constraint in §10.
Access-Control-Allow-Methods is compared as a token set: the header must list every method given, and order and spacing are not significant.
